key_insight: Using microalgae as a sacrificial agent dramatically boosts photocatalytic CO2 conversion on a polymorphic high-entropy oxide, enabling higher CO and CH4 production while keeping the process carbon-negative.
engineering_relevance: The study suggests a practical catalyst-and-feed strategy for solar-driven CO2 utilization by combining a CO2-capturing biological scavenger with a designed oxide catalyst.
method: Designed an AB2O6 high-entropy oxide, (Cs1/7Ba4/7Bi2/7)(Nb1/2Ta1/2)2O6, with layered perovskite/pyrochlore polymorphy.
Used Cs and Ba to increase surface basicity for CO2 chemisorption and Bi to promote polarization and charge separation.
Compared photocatalytic CO2 conversion with no sacrificial agent, with microplastics, and with microalgae.
evidence_signal: Compared with HEO alone, adding microalgae increased CO production by 10-fold and CH4 production by 4-fold, outperforming the microplastic-based and no-sacrificial-agent cases.
watch_item: The approach depends on maintaining microalgae viability and managing biomass handling/integration, which may complicate scale-up and reactor design.
paper_title: Sustainable photocatalytic CO2 conversion using microalgae as a carbon-negative scavenger
